AQA GCSE History 8145 · Conflict and Tension, 1918–1939

Chapter 2 · The Versailles Settlement

What did Germany lose in 1919? Why did the treaty cause such anger — and why do historians still disagree about how harsh it was?

2 detailed subtopics2 × 10-question quizzes24-question mixed quiz4 AQA-style practice tasks
2.1
Peacemaking · textbook pp. 12–13

What were the terms of the Treaty of Versailles?

The Allies dictated the final peace to Germany. The terms attacked German power through territorial losses, military restrictions, reparations and Article 231.

Date

28 June 1919

The Treaty of Versailles was signed at the Palace of Versailles, five years after the assassination of Franz Ferdinand.

German viewpoint

“Diktat”

Germany was excluded from negotiating the terms and was required to sign under the threat that fighting might resume. Many Germans regarded the settlement as dictated, not agreed.

Allied priorities

Punish · prevent · rebuild

The victors wanted Germany to compensate for damage, lose the ability to threaten its neighbours and accept a new European order.

Explore the terms · select a category

Move beyond memorising numbers: explain what each restriction did to Germany and why it mattered.

Military restrictions — precise facts

Army100,000 men; conscription banned.
Navy15,000 men, 1,500 officers and six battleships; other warships were tightly limited.
WeaponsNo tanks, submarines or air force.
RhinelandDemilitarised: Germany could not station troops or construct defences there.

Why it mattered: France hoped restrictions and the Rhineland buffer would make another German invasion harder.

Territory — key changes

Germany lost around 10% of its European territory. Alsace-Lorraine returned to France; Eupen-Malmedy went to Belgium; North Schleswig went to Denmark following a plebiscite.

The Polish Corridor gave Poland sea access but separated East Prussia from much of Germany. Danzig became a Free City under League supervision. The Saar, with valuable coalfields, was administered by the League for 15 years, with France receiving rights to the mines.

Germany also lost its overseas colonies, placed under League mandates administered by other powers.

Consequences map · clause → impact

Choose a clause and practise the explanation you would use in an 8- or 16-mark answer.

Article 231 · War Guilt Clause

Article 231 established German and allied responsibility for losses and damages caused by the war, providing a legal basis for reparations. Germans interpreted it as a humiliating declaration that they alone were to blame.

Exam precision: the text of Article 231 should not be simplified into a claim that historians agree Germany alone caused the war.

Article 232 · Reparations

The principle of paying compensation was established in 1919. The total reparations bill was fixed in 1921 at £6.6 billion (132 billion gold marks), not at the signing itself.

Germany feared the economic burden; France and other victors expected compensation for destruction and losses.

Don’t confuse these: the Saar was under League administration for 15 years; the Rhineland stayed German territory but was demilitarised; Danzig became a Free City; the Polish Corridor was transferred to Poland.

Mini timeline · 1918–1921

Fast check · which clause restricted Germany’s armed forces?

GCSE Exam Tip · 16 marks: A judgement such as “territorial losses were the worst punishment” needs evaluation. Compare territory with military weakness, reparations and war guilt; do not merely list treaty clauses. End by explaining which mattered most and why.
2.2
Peacemaking · textbook pp. 14–15

What was the reaction to the Treaty of Versailles?

Germany resented the settlement, but criticism was not limited to Germans. Cartoons and later historical interpretations show why views of the treaty differed.

German anger

The German press and public denounced the Diktat, loss of land and colonies, disarmament, responsibility for wartime damage and the burden of reparations. The new government was associated with a settlement it had not negotiated.

Criticism elsewhere

Some British commentators worried that the terms would crush Germany and destabilise Europe. Lenin condemned the treaty as victor-imposed domination. Not everyone who criticised the treaty shared the same motives.

Defence of the settlement

France had been invaded and badly damaged; many people demanded security and compensation. Some historians later argued that Germany recovered remarkably quickly, calling into question the view that Versailles permanently crippled it.

Source analysis · 4 steps

Identify message→Specific detail→Context→Inference

For a 4-mark “How do you know?” question, explain the source’s attitude, use a precise feature and connect it to events in 1919. For cartoons, describe the symbol or caption before explaining its meaning.

Provenance · 3 questions

Who? The creator and their viewpoint.

When? A 1919 reaction is different from a historian writing in 2004.

Why? A campaigning newspaper or propaganda poster may seek to persuade, while a modern historian may be reassessing later evidence.

Provenance is not a shortcut for dismissing a source as biased: explain how it affects its usefulness.

Changing judgements · select a period

Argument: treaty too harsh

Germany was excluded from negotiations and lost prestige, territory and armed forces. Resentment helped extremists exploit claims of unfair treatment. A settlement seen as unjust could fuel future grievances.

Argument: not harsh enough to prevent renewed aggression

Despite the restrictions, Germany rebuilt much of its economy during the 1920s. Later historians have argued that weak enforcement allowed Germany eventually to rearm. Neither later events nor Hitler’s propaganda automatically prove that every clause was unfair.

GCSE Exam Tip · source evaluation: Explain content, provenance and contextual knowledge. For two sources, evaluate both and make an overall assessment. Distinguish an authentic contemporary source from a later interpretation.
Think like a Grade 9 historian: “Was Versailles unfair?” and “Was Versailles effective?” are different questions. A treaty could be defensible in 1919 yet poorly enforced later — or harsh in some respects while leaving Germany capable of recovery.
